title: Harrison’s cello, Elgar’s baton
work: Cello Concerto in E minor, Op. 85 — a shared passage from the finale
question: How sharply should the cello bite into the finale’s march?
intro: At Hayes on 22 December 1919, Beatrice Harrison recorded Elgar’s finale with the composer conducting. The whole concerto was squeezed onto four shellac sides. Beside Skidmore’s complete finale, this short passage catches the cello joining the march, marked risoluto — resolute.

recordings.label: Beatrice Harrison and Edward Elgar, 1919
recordings.note: Harrison makes the concerto’s first recording with Elgar on the podium; their finale fits a single shellac side.

recordings.label: Skidmore College Orchestra
recordings.note: Skidmore plays the finale complete, allowing the cello’s late lament and the return of the concerto’s opening to unfold.

passages.label: The cello joins the march
passages.note: The soloist takes up the brisk tune, marked risoluto. Accents and little rests give it a swagger.

passages.label: The phrase climbs
passages.note: The cello climbs through a crescendo towards sharply accented high notes. The orchestra answers while the soloist pauses.

passages.label: Cello and orchestra trade places
passages.note: Short solo phrases alternate with orchestral replies. The cello’s running notes carry the march forward between its clipped accents.

alignment.timeBasis: Absolute seconds in each supplied stream; trim ends are exclusive.

maps.scope: Continuous early-finale overlap only. Excludes Skidmore’s opening introduction, all earlier Harrison movements and all later cuts.
maps.inspection: The shared passage runs continuously through the early finale. Both performances play the same music here; the excerpts end before the later cuts.
